From muse ai:  Yes, she should apply. That certificate actually changes the math. 900 out of 1000 on the SIELE is a strong score, roughly C1 across the board, and it's backed by Cervantes, UNAM, and Salamanca. That's a heavier credential than a lot of bachelor's degrees for proving Spanish ability. Two honest caveats: SIELE certs are officially valid for five years, so hers lapsed around 2023, and Mercor does list a bachelor's as a requirement. But here's why I'd still tell her to go for it. The application costs her about 30 minutes: resume plus a 20-minute AI interview. The degree line is a 'who should apply' bullet, not necessarily a hard filter, and Mercor's real gate is the bilingual competency assessment, which a native speaker with a 900 SIELE should walk through. The move is to put the SIELE front and center on the resume: 'SIELE 900/1000 (C1), Instituto Cervantes / UNAM / Universidad de Salamanca.' Worst case is silence, which costs nothing. One tip for her resume: lead with the certificate and the tutoring experience, and don't apologize for the two-year degree. The screener that matters here is the competency test, not the diploma.
* a heavier credential than a bachelor’s degree* 👊

a second option on the same site that might actually fit you better. It's called their Language and Audio Expert network. No degree requirement, just fluent Spanish and translation experience, which you have. It's not live tutoring. You'd join a pool, and when a project needs Spanish they pull you in. The work is things like writing example sentences and answers in Spanish, and grading AI translations for whether they actually sound natural. All written, on your own schedule, $35 to $50 an hour. The catch is it's a waiting list. You join once and they contact you when something matches, could be next week or a few months out. Costs nothing to join though. I'd say apply to the tutor one and join this pool too, same 20 minute interview covers both.

My apologies for the delay. I'm in Florida with the Hass' and Daniels' for a little get away to warmer weather and have been distracted by friends and fun. Very exciting possibility. General thoughts on buying a rental apartment/house (not specific to Debbie's house). 1. Depending on the market, it can be a great way to increase your investment. If you're buying at medium or low market levels, that's a total win. Buying at the higher side of the market? Less ideal. Not a dealbreaker, but less ideal. 2. Buying a rental, especially one that is well taken care of is very interesting. If you can have guaranteed rent coming in to help pay for mortgage huge win! Does Debbie's elerkin property have two rentals? 3. Would you be looking to move out and live in whatever place your bought or are you thinking of buying something from the investment opportunity? 4. While 6% interest loan isn't the worst, it's definitely not great. Back in 2020, people were locking in 3% interests for 30 years. Granted, things have obviously changed, but I'd speak with more people about interest on loans before moving forward. People with lots of loan experience from buying multiple properties like Kevin Daniels, Carson Smith, Pat Wilbur. Send any of them an email with questions regarding interest rates, loans, even buying a rental they'll be able to give you some good advice. 5. Buying a house is a ton of responsibility especially as a rental. You have maintenance, insurance, taxes, tenants, leases, etc., plus obviously the financial responsibility of it. That said, being single, having a good job, being able to put in overtime to make extra money to pay off the house quicker is a great time to take on this responsibility. If you could work your butt off, live like a pauper, and pay the house off in 5+ years, that would be epic! Imagine you put $25k a year towards the house. It would take you 5-7 years to pay off. And rental income would pay taxes, upkeep, insurance, and interest. So your $25k would go right to the principal.

Now, as far as purchasing from Debbie specifically: 1. Purchases are negotiations. You're going to have to negotiate for the best price possible. 2. Debbie knows the market, so she's going to fight (rightfully so) for what she believes/knows is a good price. 3. She will make more money if she doesn't need to use a realtor so that's something to keep in mind when negotiating. 4. If your dad is willing to help with the negotiating process, definitely worth considering. You wouldn't want to go at this alone.

Other Thoughts: 1. Kevin Daniels has said before that buying a house that has less than three apartments is hard to make money. Might be worth talking to him before going much further. 2. There is a guy at CFC, Gabe Vergara (maybe you've heard of him), who is Airforce Reserves I believe. Anyways, his background is loans for houses specializing in military loans. I texted him and he is eager to talk to you. You can text him (or maybe just call him) at: 1 (808) 726-0606.

Yes, you definitely want to think through all of the implications. If nothing else, this is a great opportunity to learn a lot. I d say lean into the opportunity to gain knowledge and understanding, even if it doesn t lead to you purchasing a house right now.

katerina cavellos.name: Katerina Cavellos
msgs: Understanding Actions and True Intentions At its core, the idea is that actions speak louder than words: we often use a person s behavior and its outcomes to guess their real motives. Psychological research supports this: Correspondent Inference Theory (an attribution theory) notes that when we see someone behaving intentionally in distinctive ways, we tend to attribute those actions to their inner traits or motives . For example, if a colleague helps a stranger, we instinctively infer they are kind . Likewise, observers assume an action with a positive result implies benevolence, while a negative result implies selfishness or malice . In fact, Carl Jung (and later Jordan Peterson) famously advised: If you cannot understand why someone did something, look at the consequences and infer the motive . On the one hand, this is a common-sense guideline: someone s life outcomes and how they treat others can be powerful clues to what they truly want. On the other hand, critics warn this is only a hypothesis, not proof , and can tempt us into unfounded guesses. Behavioral and Cognitive Foundations Behavioral psychology emphasizes that rewards and punishments shape future actions. Over time, the consistent outcomes of our actions reflect what we value: if a behavior reliably yields comfort or approval, we re likely motivated to repeat it. In cognitive terms, our minds are wired to fill in gaps. We don t just see a smile or a helped person, we ask why. The process of attribution means we infer underlying intentions from observable facts . Because mental states are invisible, we rely on consequences as evidence. If someone s behavior repeatedly leads to positive outcomes for others, we assume goodwill; repeated harm suggests hostile intent . Indeed, evolutionary psychology suggests this is adaptive: humans evolved to detect deception and hidden motives for survival . For example, a salesperson s empty smile is seen as disingenuous because we ve learned to spot cues when someone is trying to sell rather than be friendly . Over eons, our guess intentions from effects skill became part of our defense system, helping us avoid being fooled . Cognitive research also shows that people struggle to know their own motives. The introspection illusion and cognitive dissonance reveal that we often rationalize our actions after the fact. When someone acts against their stated values, they feel discomfort and then explain or alter beliefs to reduce that dissonance . For instance, if you promise to eat healthy but end up binging junk food, you might blame stress or say I deserved it, rather than admit a wish to indulge. This means we (and others) may not truly know why an action happened, only that it did. Observers, however, will notice the action and outcome: thus third-parties infer motive from behavior, whether or not the actor understands it. Evolutionary Perspective From an evolutionary vantage, reading motivations in others was crucial. Our ancestors needed to know who was trustworthy or dangerous. Over time, humans developed a keen eye for patterns: a friendly villager who suddenly attacked reveals aggression; one who always shares reveals generosity. Scholars note that part of our evolved defense system against deception is detecting underlying intentions . In modern terms, this shows up as the gut feeling you get when someone s actions don t match their words. We unconsciously track behavioral patterns and infer motives because doing so helped our ancestors survive and cooperate. Thus, many claims that people eventually show their true colors have roots in how our brains evolved to spot honest versus hidden agendas. Everyday Life and Relationships In personal relationships and major life decisions, people often say that behavior is the best indicator of priorities. For example, consider someone who never replies to texts. A common interpretation is that they lack interest or respect. According to approach-avoidance conflict theory, however, the picture can be complex . A person might want to reply (approach the reward of connection) but feel anxiety or fear at the thought of confrontation or rejection (avoidance) . This inner conflict can freeze them into inaction. Similarly, someone may pass on a promotion not because they don t want success, but because their avoidance of stress outweighs their desire for advancement . Still, in many scenarios people do use outcomes as crude signals. In relationships, behavioral cues are powerful. If a partner repeatedly fails to show up, ignores requests, or doesn t compromise, these outcomes signal their true investment level. As author Mark Manson puts it, Your actions (staying with them) speak louder than any of your words ( don t cheat on me ) possibly could . In other words, saying I care about you means little if every action suggests indifference. In life decisions, the same applies: someone who says they value health but never exercises or eat better may actually fear failure more than they desire fitness. Each day-to-day choice (job acceptance, spending time, even small habits) reflects underlying motivations or hesitations. Patterns emerge: if you consistently date people who abandon you, Jung s shovel would say you subconsciously want abandonment. In reality, as one psychologist illustrates, that pattern might reflect ingrained preferences or family models, not a conscious wish . Still, friends might understandably point to the outcome and suspect some hidden self-sabotage. Complicating Factors Fear and Anxiety: Emotions like fear can override pure intention. Approach-avoidance research shows that fear tends to spike as one nears a decision, often blocking action . For example, fear of conflict can keep a person from speaking up even if they deeply care. This means outcomes (e.g. silence) may not reflect a lack of desire but fear of consequences . Situational Constraints: External factors (financial needs, social pressure, legal rules) often dictate behavior. Someone may want to travel the world but can t afford it; they may seem unambitious, yet the constraint masks their motivation. Likewise, social norms or jobs may force people to act against their preferences (e.g. working overtime to keep a boss s approval), so outcomes can mislead about true wishes. Conflicting Desires: People usually have multiple motivations that push in different directions. Internal conflicts (like wanting to eat cake but also stay healthy) can produce inconsistent actions. Cognitive dissonance research shows that when actions and values clash, people often change their stated motives rather than admit conflict . This means the outcome you see (someone eating cake) might either reflect indulgence or a rationalization, not a single true motive. Attribution Biases: We also tend to commit the fundamental attribution error attributing others actions too much to personality and not enough to circumstances. For instance, if a co-worker misses a deadline, we might think they re lazy, but it could be due to high workload or personal issues. Studies note that when consequences are strong, we tend more toward attributing actions to stable personality traits rather than situational factors , which can lead to unfair judgments. These points show that while outcomes can hint at motives, the link is imperfect. Jordan Peterson himself often quotes Jung s maxim , but critics caution that it is the worst kind of speculation an unfalsifiable guess that sounds logical but may be wrong . In sum, behavior is informative but not infallible for reading intent. Insights from Modern Psychologists Several contemporary thinkers echo or refine these ideas. Jordan Peterson (citing Jung) suggests looking at consequences to understand motives , while Mark Manson bluntly notes that actions ultimately reveal our true tolerances and values in relationships . Bren Brown, champion of authenticity, emphasizes that what we do each day the choices we have to make to show up real defines who we are, implying that genuine behavior (not empty talk) builds trust. (As she puts it, authenticity is a collection of choices that we have to make every day. ) Similarly, Simon Sinek s popular mantra people don t buy what you do; they buy why you do it highlights that demonstrable motives matter. These voices remind us that discerning motive from outcome is a common human theme: it underlies advice from first dates ( judge character by their actions ) to leadership ( lead by example ). One fresh perspective is the self-fulfilling prophecy of attribution. Psychological research warns that if we treat someone according to the motive we inferred, we may elicit confirming behavior . In one study, a police officer assumed residents were tough while they assumed the officer was aggressive; each behaved in ways that confirmed the other s bias . In daily life, if you decide My friend is lazy because they never invite me out, you might stop offering invitations. That friend might then drift away further, seeming to prove your point. In reality, you may have created the distance. Thus, our inferences can influence outcomes, blurring cause and effect. Conclusion In sum, there is truth to the notion that people s outcomes in life and relationships can reveal underlying motivations. Behavioral patterns and consequences offer valuable clues, and our brains naturally use them to make sense of others. Evolution and psychology suggest this tendency is adaptive it helped us navigate social life. However, one must be cautious: fear, context, and inner conflict can distort simple readings of behavior. As Jung s so-called shovel demonstrates, inferring motive from outcome is at best a hypothesis . A truly comprehensive understanding requires dialogue and empathy: checking our assumptions, considering external factors, and being open to multiple motives. By doing so, we respect both the power and the limits of the principle actions speak louder than words, integrating insight from psychology with real-world compassion. Sources: Contemporary psychology research on attribution and motivation ; writing by Jordan Peterson and others on behavior and motive ; and applied examples from relationship counseling and behavioral theory .

If the Model Y s still qualify for the tax credit that could be interesting as well. I ve driven them- they re very similar to the M3 s with layout, etc. I m unsure with a tax credit if they d be more comparable in price or not, but 2023 s had some good discounts on them last I saw. Loved Rest in peace, Norma Louise (Stewart) Meyers. Grandma provided a continuous stability for our family, always being mindful of birthdays and holidays, and always being very generous. We re grateful that she was with us for a few months and that she was well taken care of.

Emphasized The first week here has been really good so far. It still feels a bit like waiting for the other shoe to drop because classes start on Monday, and that s when the real work begins. But it s been nice having a dorm with just three people instead of 30. It s also nice having access to a tablet and my AirPods in the evenings. The mornings are still early, but I m getting much better sleep and no longer waking up in the middle of the night. I m also about 95% back to normal health. They have vending machines that we re allowed to use during personal time in the barracks, and we re also permitted to use the beverage vending machines at the schoolhouse. I ll have to be careful not to go broke or gain too much weight. A Celsius in the morning is a must to keep from falling asleep. They take dozing off in class very seriously you can get written up for it. Two write-ups result in an Article 15 (military law). The platoon size dynamic is a bit different here. In BCT, there were four platoons of about 55 people each. We did most things together, so that meant 220 people moving at once, which made everything slower. Our platoon here is larger 74 people but the platoons are much more independent. They function like their own mini companies, so things like getting through chow happen a lot faster. One thing I didn t see coming (but maybe should have) is that Human Resources is heavily female-dominated. There are 74 people in the platoon, but only 17 are male. Not sure if that will affect the dynamic at all. I had the fastest two-mile time in our platoon, which was nice. A not-so-nice part is that the fastest runner has to carry the guidon (the small flag at the end of a wooden pole). It s not terrible, but it does mean I m at the front of all formations and have to carry the pole with me everywhere. In Week 5, we should be transitioning to Gold Phase, which will allow us to move around post. That means we ll be able to go to stores, barbershops, Panda Express, and I think there s a movie theater. The last two weeks are considered Gold+ Phase, during which we re allowed to go off-post for the day. Classes start on Monday. We had a brief orientation at the schoolhouse today. It s structured a lot like college, but we can t take any notes out of the classroom to prevent cheating. They also start our GPA at 100 instead of 0. You can t drop below 80%, or you risk getting recycled or removed. The quizzes are all open-book on the laptops, though, so I m feeling pretty good about it.
